title: Hydrodynamics of two-dimensional electrons due to scattering by disorder
authors: D. R. Raskulov, K. A. Baryshnikov, P. S. Alekseev
abstract: The hydrodynamic regime of electron transport, induced by fast inter-electron collisions, was discovered in high-quality nanostructures in recent ten years. However, signs of hydrodynamic transport, primarily, the giant negative magnetoresistance, were observed even at very low temperatures, when electron-electron scattering is too weak to affect the transport. To address this puzzle, here we develop a theory of mixed, hydrodynamic and non-Markovian, magnetotransport of two-dimensional electrons at zero temperature in samples with weak but still important disorder. Namely, we account for both the memory effects at electron scattering by localized defects in magnetic field and an unconventional viscosity effect due to electron scattering by defects in bulk and by rough sample edges. Solution of the model yields a strong negative magnetoresistance, which exhibits at zero magnetic field a sharp maximum in narrower samples or a blunt maximum in wider samples. This and other our results explain various properties of the giant negative magnetoresistance observed on ultra-high-quality GaAs quantum wells, thereby we apparently reveal the nature of low-temperature magnetotransport in these systems.
summary: This work develops a comprehensive theory for magnetotransport in 2D electron systems by combining memory effects from localized disorder scattering with hydrodynamic viscosity. The model successfully explains the observed giant negative magnetoresistance in high-quality quantum wells, distinguishing between narrow and wide sample regimes based on the relative dominance of these two physical mechanisms.
main_problem: The paper addresses the puzzle of observing hydrodynamic-like transport signatures, such as giant negative magnetoresistance, in 2D electron systems even when electron-electron scattering is too weak to cause them conventionally.
main_result: The developed theory successfully explains the observed giant negative magnetoresistance by modeling the mixed transport regime involving both memory effects from localized defects and unconventional viscosity from bulk/edge scattering.
method: The authors developed a theoretical model using phenomenological balance transport equations for two types of electrons (circling and traveling) and solved them in the stationary regime.
model_or_system: The system is two-dimensional electron gas in high-quality nanostructures, such as GaAs quantum wells, subjected to weak disorder. The model incorporates memory effects and hydrodynamic viscosity arising from scattering mechanisms.
key_observables: Magnetoresistance ($ho_{xx}(B)$), exhibiting characteristic sharp peaks (narrow samples) or blunt maxima (wide samples) at zero magnetic field.
important_parameters: Sample width ($W$), magnetic field ($B$), temperature ($T$), and characteristic scattering/transition lengths ($l_{tc}, l_G$).
main_assumptions: The model assumes the existence of two electron populations (c- and t-electrons) and uses approximations like the gradual channel approximation and stationary flow conditions.
figures_summary: Figures compare the model's predictions for $ho_{xx}$ vs. $B$ (showing characteristic shapes) against experimental measurements from GaAs quantum wells, demonstrating agreement in both narrow and wide sample limits.
paper_structure: The paper develops the theory by formulating balance equations for electron densities and flows, deriving analytical expressions for $ho_{xx}$ in different sample width limits, and finally comparing these theoretical predictions across various regimes (low/high B, narrow/wide W) against experimental data.
why_interesting: The detailed modeling of non-Markovian transport and the explicit separation of memory and hydrodynamic contributions provide a rich framework for understanding transport in disordered quantum systems, which is relevant to open quantum systems dynamics.
